newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Cavallo says "mission accomplished" on crime rings.
newsitem.headline: Cavallo says "mission accomplished" on crime rings.

text.p: Former Argentine economy minister Domingo Cavallo declared Sunday "mission accomplished" in his anti-corruption campaign against postal tycoon Alfredo Yabran and said he would now concentrate on his independent political campaign.

"I have decided to close this chapter. The country needed its eyes to be opened against the 'mafia' and organized crime. It was tough, but feel like I have won because society is now fully conscious," he told La Nacion. Cavallo uses the word "mafia" to refer to crime rings.

Cavallo, sacked last July by President Carlos Menem after bringing Argentina unaccustomed economic stability, has been denouncing Yabran since mid-1995, forcing the secretive businessman to emerge into the media spotlight this week to refute Cavallo's charges.

In interviews with La Nacion and Clarin newspapers published Sunday, the man once known as Menem's "Superminister" said he had accomplished "a tough mission" and would now leave it up to the courts to probe Yabran.

Cavallo accuses the enigmatic businessman of being the leader of a crime syndicate allegedly trying to build up monopolies in the postal sector and in airport services for criminal purposes. He has also accused two government ministers and senior judges of giving Yabran protection. All are suing him.

To Clarin, Cavallo celebrated the fact that Congress now plans to set up a committee to investigate Yabran's business: "I'm very glad because transparency is to the mafia like light is to vampires. At the same time, it will be very difficult now for the courts not to investigate racketeering and mafias."
Yabran denied all of Cavallo's charges in this week's media interviews and accused him in turn of acting as a "covert operator" for foreign companies.

Cavallo alleges Yabran is powerful figure behind the scenes in Argentine business and told Clarin: "In 25 years he set up an organization with deep penetration into political power." He said members of both the ruling Peronist Party and opposition Radical Party were in Yabran's pocket.

The former minister plans to run as an independent candidate in mid-term elections in October this year and is considering trying for the presidency in 1999, promoting his reputation as a "man of action" in Argentine politics.

"I can provide leadership because I have shown I am a man of action," he told La Nacion, defining his role as giving Argentines a new political alternative in October's Congressional vote and in 1999.
He is also betting on his reputation as the man who brought Argentines economic and monetary stability and free-market reforms. "With me, people won't be afraid of returning to inflation."
